title: Is the biggest pack the best deal?
hook: Three bags of rice. Surely the biggest one is cheapest per gram?

doesNotKnow: that the biggest pack is not always the cheapest per gram
that the rate, price divided by size, is what compares packs

misconception: Bigger packs are always better value.
objective: The learner can compare packs by dividing price by size, and explain that the rate need not fall as the pack grows.

claims.source: 350 / 5 = 70 cents; 510 / 7.5 = 68 cents; 840 / 12 = 70 cents. Demo.tsx per100(cents, grams).

claims.text: Of the three, the 750 g pack is cheapest per 100 g, and the 1.2 kg pack costs the same rate as the 500 g pack.
On the slider, the 1.2 kg pack's price per 100 g is its shelf price divided by 12 (for example $8.16 gives $0.68).
claims.source: 1200 g / 100 g = 12; 816 / 12 = 68 cents. Slider runs $7.20 to $9.60 in $0.12 steps (one cent per 100 g).

claims.text: The prices are invented, not real shop prices; a unit price ignores waste and storage.
claims.source: Stage chip 'Made-up prices'; reveal's last line.

recall.question: Coffee: 250 g for $5.00 or 1 kg for $22.00. Which costs less per 100 g?
options: The 1 kg bag, because bigger is cheaper
They cost the same per 100 g
recall.why: $5.00 / 2.5 = $2.00 per 100 g; $22.00 / 10 = $2.20 per 100 g. Divide price by size; the rate need not fall as the pack grows.
